question: Current legislation does not allow the value of products under conversion to organic farming to be enhanced by means of a special status, with the exception of plants consisting of a single raw material and in their second or third year of conversion.

What is more, the organic certification label is facing growing competition from less rigorous certifications, such as the HVE (high environmental value) label in France. These certifications make similar claims to the organic certification, but meet fewer specifications, misleading consumers and weakening the organic sector, which is already struggling. 1.
Is there a way that products under conversion can obtain a distinct status with a view to supporting farmers transitioning to the organic sector?

Is the Commission planning to regulate certification labels such as ‘HVE’? The use of ‘produced in [Member State]’ can be misleading for some consumers and therefore goes against Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, as it mainly refers to the country where the last substantial processing of the product took place.
Is the Commission planning to impose a requirement that at least 50% of the value of a food product must come from the Member State concerned for this claim to be made?
answer: To facilitate the transition, considerable EU financial support is available to farmers who undertake conversion to organic farming.

Nevertheless, to avoid the risk of confusing and misleading the consumers, Regulation (EU) 2018/848 (1) provides that products produced during the conversion period cannot be sold as ‘in conversion products’, with the exception of plant reproductive material, food products of plant origin and feed products of plant origin that have only one agricultural crop ingredient after a conversion period of at least one year.

The directive Empowering consumers for the green transition (2), which amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (3), sets general principles to protect consumers from misleading sustainability claims and unreliable labelling schemes. Moreover, the Commission proposed the ‘Green claims directive’ to ensure that environmental labels and claims are credible and trustworthy.

In addition, any certification schemes endorsed by Member States are to be notified under the procedure established by Directive 2015/1535 (4), and their compliance with EU law is assessed accordingly. Under Regulation 1169/2011 (5) food information shall not be misleading, particularly by suggesting that the food possesses special characteristics when in fact all similar foods possess them.
The Commission is not considering the amendment of the definition of the country of origin for foods.

Under Regulation 1169/2011 goods whose production involved more than one country are deemed to originate in the country where they underwent their last, substantial, economically justified processing or working in an undertaking equipped for that purpose and resulting in the manufacture of a new product or representing an important stage of manufacture.
